metadata.title: PIRLS 2006 Assessment Framework and Specifications
metadata.venue: TIMSS & PIRLS International Study Center, Boston College

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This document is a framework and specifications blueprint for the PIRLS 2006 assessment rather than an empirical analysis paper. It describes the assessment design (matrix sampling with 13 student booklets, 80 minutes of test time plus a 15–30 minute student questionnaire) and the use of item response theory methods to place responses on a common scale for reporting. Because no student-level dataset is analyzed here, the manuscript does not specify the application of complex survey weights (e.g., student sampling weights) or replicate-weight procedures. For analysts using PIRLS microdata, the appropriate approach is to follow IEA’s PIRLS sampling and scaling documentation for weighting and variance estimation, since PIRLS uses a complex sampling design and matrix sampling to reduce individual burden.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This is a framework/specifications document that does not estimate models on student microdata outcomes, so plausible values (PV) handling and missing-data handling strategies for PV-based achievement are not part of the reported methodology. The document focuses on defining reading literacy, specifying test content (passages, question types, scoring), and describing how responses are scaled for reporting. As a result, there is no reporting of PV generation/combining rules or missing-data procedures for an empirical analysis.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: No analytic student sample is constructed in this framework document. It specifies the target population as students in their fourth year of formal schooling (ISCED Level 1), with an additional constraint to avoid assessing students below a minimum average age (9.5 years at the time of testing for PIRLS 2001). It also specifies the test administration structure (matrix sampling across 10 blocks, 13 booklets, 80 minutes of testing plus a student questionnaire) but does not provide inclusion/exclusion rules for an empirical analytic dataset.

data.outcome_summary: This document specifies the PIRLS 2006 assessment framework for measuring reading literacy in students’ fourth year of formal schooling. Reading literacy is defined as the ability to understand and use written language forms, and the assessment covers three aspects: comprehension processes, purposes for reading, and reading behaviors/attitudes via questionnaires. The written test uses authentic literary and informational passages, with comprehension assessed through four comprehension processes (focus/retrieve explicitly stated information; make straightforward inferences; interpret/integrate ideas; examine/evaluate content, language, and textual elements) and two purposes (literary experience; acquire/use information). Test items are delivered using matrix sampling: passages and items are divided into 10 blocks (L1–L5 and I1–I5) and distributed across 13 booklets, limiting individual burden to 80 minutes plus a 15–30 minute student questionnaire. After data collection, responses are placed on a common scale using item response theory methods for reporting overall reading literacy and separate scales by purpose and process.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This is a framework/specifications report, not an empirical study estimating predictive models or reporting model performance on student outcomes. Therefore, fields such as total_students, per-country analytic Ns, PV handling details for achievement modeling, missing-data handling for an analysis dataset, and ML techniques are not applicable to the document’s purpose. The document does, however, provide detailed assessment design information (matrix sampling, item types, scoring procedures, and scaling approach) that would be used in the subsequent PIRLS 2006 international report analyses.
